subject: design-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In designing, what is a 'design context'?
options: The situation, setting or circumstances in which a product will be used
A detailed technical drawing of the final product
A list of the exact materials a product must be made from
The selling price agreed with the client
questions.explain: A design context describes the setting or situation from which design problems and opportunities are identified.

questions.q: A design brief is best described as:
options: A concise statement outlining the problem and what the designer is expected to do
A finished evaluation of the completed product
A costed list of every component used in manufacture
A questionnaire given to potential users
questions.explain: The brief sets out the problem, the intended user or client and the designer's task before detailed work begins.

questions.q: Why do designers begin by exploring a design context rather than an idea?
options: It helps identify genuine problems and opportunities to design for
It guarantees the product will be cheap to make
It removes the need to carry out any research
It fixes the final dimensions of the product
questions.explain: Analysing a context reveals real needs and opportunities, giving the design a clear purpose.

questions.q: Who is the 'client' for a product?
options: The person or organisation who commissions the product
The factory worker who assembles the product
The shop that sells the product to the public
The material supplier
questions.explain: The client commissions and often pays for the work, and may differ from the person who actually uses the product.

questions.q: Why is it important to distinguish between the client and the user?
options: The client commissions the product but the user may have different needs to satisfy
The client and user are always the same person
Only the client's opinion matters in design
Users never affect how a product is designed
questions.explain: The client and end user can be different people, so the designer must consider the needs of both.

questions.q: Which of these is primary research?
options: Carrying out a questionnaire with potential users
Reading a published market report
Looking up statistics in a textbook
Using data from an existing website
questions.explain: Primary research is first-hand data the designer gathers themselves, such as questionnaires, interviews and observation.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of secondary research?
options: Reading existing books, websites or published market data
Interviewing users face to face
Observing people using a product
Disassembling a competitor's product yourself
questions.explain: Secondary research uses information already collected and published by others.

questions.q: A designer takes apart an existing kettle to study how it is made. This is an example of:
options: Primary research through product analysis
Secondary research from a book
Writing a manufacturing specification
Producing a design brief
questions.explain: Disassembly and product analysis are first-hand investigations, making them a form of primary research.

questions.q: What does the term 'anthropometrics' refer to?
options: The measurement of human body sizes and proportions
The study of how much a product costs to make
The testing of a material's strength
The environmental impact of a product
questions.explain: Anthropometric data records human body measurements so products can be sized to fit users.

questions.q: Ergonomics is best defined as the study of:
options: The relationship between people and the products or environments they use
The chemical composition of materials
The cost of manufacturing a product
The lifespan of a battery
questions.explain: Ergonomics considers how easily and comfortably people can interact with a product.

questions.q: Why do designers often use the 5th to 95th percentile range of anthropometric data?
options: To accommodate the majority of the population, around 90% of users
To fit only the largest possible person
To design solely for the average person
To reduce the number of measurements needed
questions.explain: Designing between the 5th and 95th percentiles suits about 90% of users, a practical compromise.

questions.q: A designer is setting the height of a wall-mounted light switch so that most people can reach it. Which anthropometric data is most relevant?
options: Vertical reach of users, using a low percentile so shorter people can reach
Foot length of users
Head circumference of users
Hand grip strength of users
questions.explain: Using a lower-percentile reach ensures even shorter users can operate the switch.

questions.q: A student wants to find out which features teenagers most want in a school bag. Which is the most appropriate primary research method?
options: A questionnaire or survey of teenagers
Reading a published report on adult luggage sales
Copying data from a manufacturer's website
Estimating what they think teenagers want
questions.explain: Directly surveying the target users gives relevant first-hand information about their needs.

questions.q: A design specification is:
options: A list of criteria and requirements the finished product must meet
The final selling price of the product
A sketch of the first idea
A record of the tools used in the workshop
questions.explain: The design specification lists measurable criteria, drawn from research, that the product must satisfy.

questions.q: Why should points in a design specification be measurable where possible?
options: So the product can be objectively tested and evaluated against them
So the specification takes longer to write
So the client cannot understand it
So no research is needed
questions.explain: Measurable criteria allow the finished product to be tested fairly against clear targets.

questions.q: Which of these is a well-written, measurable specification point?
options: The product must weigh no more than 500 grams
The product should be quite light
The product must look nice
The product should be a good size
questions.explain: A measurable, quantified criterion like a maximum weight can be tested objectively, unlike vague statements.

questions.q: In the ACCESS FM checklist often used to structure a specification, what does the 'F' stand for?
options: Function
Finish
Fabric
Fashion
questions.explain: ACCESS FM stands for Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Size, Safety, Function and Materials.

questions.q: How does a manufacturing specification differ from a design specification?
options: It gives detailed technical information needed to actually make the product
It only lists the user's opinions
It is written before any research is done
It replaces the need for a design brief
questions.explain: A manufacturing specification provides precise technical details such as dimensions, tolerances and processes for production.

questions.q: Research shows users want a torch that survives being dropped and is easy to hold in the dark. Which specification point best captures this?
options: The casing must withstand a drop from 1 metre and have a textured, non-slip grip
The torch should be reasonably tough and comfy
The torch must look modern
The torch should be popular with customers
questions.explain: This point is specific and testable, directly translating the research findings into measurable criteria.

questions.q: A designer needs reliable information about the target market's spending habits but has limited time. Which approach is most suitable?
options: Use existing published market data as secondary research
Individually interview several hundred people
Guess the figures based on personal opinion
Ignore the market and design for themselves
questions.explain: Published market data is a quick, credible secondary source when time for first-hand research is limited.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) Design & Technology (J310) specification; Identifying Requirements
